title: Fleet Management (Multi-Robot)
contentStatus: Built per Content Principles (60% pass, terminology + notes). Fleet-wide dashboard view specifics pending SME confirmation (overlaps Module 3's dashboard question).

sections.title: From One Unit to a Fleet
learningObjectives: Understand why multiple MoRo units are deployed together
Recognize the operational shift from single-unit to fleet thinking
sections.content: Everything so far has addressed operating a single MoRo unit. Many deployments run multiple units simultaneously - for throughput (more units moving more material) or redundancy (coverage continues if one unit is down for maintenance). Fleet management is about thinking at the level of the whole operation, not just one robot.

keyTerms.note: MoRo's Human-Machine Interface (HMI) platform, used for fleet monitoring, mission control, and programming.

sections.title: Collision Avoidance Across Units
learningObjectives: Understand the general principle of multi-robot collision avoidance
Recognize that this is handled automatically, not by the operator
sections.content: When multiple MoRo units share a floor, each is aware of the others' positions and coordinates paths to avoid collisions - this is handled by the fleet management system automatically, not something an operator manages manually. Your role is awareness that this coordination is happening, not active involvement in it.

sections.title: Task Assignment Across a Fleet
learningObjectives: Understand the general principle of how work gets distributed across units
Recognize the operator's role in fleet-level task assignment
sections.content: With multiple units available, the fleet system distributes missions based on factors like proximity, availability, and current load - again, largely automatic rather than something the operator manually assigns unit-by-unit. The exact fleet-wide dashboard view and assignment interface will be confirmed against DiFacto's ANT documentation.

sections.title: Zone Management
learningObjectives: Understand the concept of reserved routes and shared paths
Recognize why zone management matters at fleet scale
sections.content: As unit count increases, some areas of the floor may be designated as shared paths (multiple units can pass through, coordinated automatically) versus reserved routes (prioritized for specific traffic patterns). This zone structure exists to keep throughput efficient as fleet size grows - understanding that it exists helps you interpret fleet behavior that might otherwise look unusual.

keyTerms.note: A floor route multiple MoRo units can use, with automatic coordination to avoid conflicts.
A floor route prioritized or dedicated for specific traffic patterns within the fleet.

sections.title: Deadlock Situations
learningObjectives: Understand what a deadlock is in a multi-robot context
Know that the system is designed to resolve deadlocks automatically
sections.content: A deadlock occurs when two or more units reach a situation where each is waiting on the other to move first, with neither able to proceed. The fleet system is designed to detect and resolve this automatically - typically by directing one unit to reroute. If you observe units that appear mutually stalled for longer than expected, that's worth flagging rather than assuming it will always self-resolve.

keyTerms.note: A situation where two or more units are each waiting on the other, with neither able to proceed without intervention.

sections.title: Monitoring Multiple Units
learningObjectives: Understand the general concept of a fleet-wide dashboard view
Recognize the shift in monitoring approach at fleet scale
sections.content: Monitoring a fleet means watching for patterns across units rather than tracking any single unit continuously - a unit that deviates from the fleet's normal behavior stands out precisely because you understand what normal looks like across the group. The specific fleet-wide view in ANT will be confirmed and detailed once verified against the live system.

questions.question: Why might multiple MoRo units be deployed together?
options: It's never done - one unit per facility
questions.feedback: Correct. Multiple units support both higher throughput and redundant coverage.

questions.question: Who manages collision avoidance between multiple MoRo units?
options: Each unit independently, with no coordination
questions.feedback: Correct. Collision avoidance across units is handled automatically by the fleet system.

questions.question: What is a deadlock in a multi-robot context?
options: A situation where units are each waiting on the other, with neither proceeding
questions.feedback: Correct. A deadlock is a mutual-wait situation between units, typically resolved automatically.

questions.question: What's the difference between a shared path and a reserved route?
options: Shared paths allow multiple coordinated units; reserved routes are prioritized for specific traffic
Reserved routes are only for maintenance
questions.feedback: Correct. Shared paths coordinate multiple units; reserved routes prioritize specific traffic patterns.

questions.question: What does monitoring a fleet primarily involve?
options: Tracking one unit continuously and ignoring the rest
Watching for patterns and deviations across units
questions.feedback: Correct. Fleet monitoring is about recognizing deviation from normal group behavior.
